 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
 The PCB has refused permission for Pakistan's over-50s team to play in India .
 Pakistan won the last edition of the International Masters Cricket World Cup in Sri Lanka.
 Organisers have been told to arrange a replacement side for the January tournament.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Pakistan pull out of International Masters Cricket World Cup in India
 Pakistan will not take part in the International Masters Cricket World Cup in India next January after the Pakistan Cricket Board declined a request from the country's over-50s team to travel, a decision that removes the defending champions from the tournament.
 The Pakistan Veterans Cricket Association had sought clearance to compete, having won the previous edition in Sri Lanka last year, but the board informed them they are not permitted to play in India. Fawad Ijaz, who heads the PVCA, confirmed the withdrawal on Wednesday.
 He said: "We have informed the organisers about our withdrawal from the World Cup so that they can arrange for an alternate team."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement MORE:  Akhtar recalls how Flintoff's Tarzan-Jane insult came back to haunt England star 
 Why the PCB blocked Pakistan's veterans from travelling to India
 The PVCA had done the groundwork before approaching the authorities, and Ijaz said the organisers and the host nation had given assurances on both visas and high-level security for the squad. Only after receiving those guarantees did the association seek permission from the PCB and from the Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Interior.
 The answer came from Mohsin Naqvi, Pakistan's interior minister, who also heads the PCB. Ijaz revealed that Naqvi informed them they would not be allowed to play in India, which effectively ended the matter regardless of what the organisers had offered.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement It is not an isolated case either. The Pakistan Hockey Federation recently refused to travel to India for the Asian Champions Trophy and was replaced by Bangladesh, and the two countries have long restricted their cricketing contact to multi-nation events at neutral venues because of strained political relations.
 MORE:  Stunning batting, destructive bowling: How 'superstar' Arafat Minhas single-handedly floored Harry Brook's England 
 A veterans tournament is the wrong place to draw this line
 The reasoning behind keeping senior teams apart in bilateral cricket is well established by now, and no board is going to override its own government on a matter of travel clearance. Naqvi wears both hats here, which made the outcome fairly predictable once the request reached him.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement What does not hold up is applying that logic to an over-50s competition. This is not a bilateral series or a contest with ranking points attached, and the PVCA had already secured written assurances on visas and security, which were the two practical objections anyone could raise.
 The people who lose out are the players themselves, most of whom will not get another crack at a World Cup at this stage of their lives, and a tournament that is now scrambling for a replacement side weeks before it begins. If the point was to make a political statement, a group of retired cricketers in their fifties is an odd place to make it.
